pull_request.title: Software: Validate Python-first ACTS module geometry and propagation
pull_request.head: study/pyacts-gen3-bindings
pull_request.body:
Finite sensitive modules can now be constructed directly in Python and placed into Gen-3 blueprints. This addresses the expert review's question about requiring JSON: module placement and blueprint topology are Python code; JSON remains an explicit compatibility and regression control.

The `pyacts==47.7.0` wheel lacks `Surface.assignIsSensitive` and single-surface JSON converter bindings. Its vector reader was the original workaround. The local corrected ACTS main checkout fixes the historical transform constructor but still lacked the setter. [ACTS PR #6176](https://github.com/acts-project/acts/pull/6176) adds that existing C++ method to Python, with regression tests and unchanged placement-ownership semantics.

Validation on the patched local ACTS build:
- 32 sensitive modules with unique IDs in two barrel and two disc layers.
- Baseline and alternating-z fixtures, both TryAll and SurfaceArray: 1,600 analytic ray comparisons, with exact native/JSON identifiers and navigation output.
- 48 tracks per 0/2 T case and backend: 192 checked propagations, with exact native/JSON written paths and 34/30 module intersections per field case. Every generated track is accounted for. Repeated seeded controls are not independent statistical samples.
- Four added ACTS test cases fail before the binding patch; 20 focused tests pass after it. With the user's dependency update, the full Python Core suite passes: 56 passed, 1 skipped. All ACTS pre-commit hooks pass.
- Original wheel controls still pass. nODD dashboard tests (27), session/document tests (32), log validation and dashboard validation/build pass.

Review/reproduction:
- [Expert response and capability boundary](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/docs/validation/TRK-SE03-pyacts-bindings.md)
- [Python-first runner and commands](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/tools/acts_binding_probe/README.md)
- [Retained native/JSON evidence](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/docs/validation/TRK-SE03-python-construction.json)
- [Historical propagation figure](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/docs/validation/figures/TRK-SE03-propagation-xy.png); earlier reports remain unchanged.

This is an isolated software prototype under DES-005 / TRK-SE03. It does not select a detector layout, establish hermeticity or authorize production geometry. Real masks/stereo, material, field maps, beamspot coverage, response and reconstruction remain open. Geant4 setup reports a missing data directory; no Geant4 transport validation is claimed.

comments.body:
Hi @paulgessinger - can you please review this one ?

The task was to find out if `pyacts 47.7` is sufficient enough to do Gen-3 geometry building and propagation tests.
This is preparatory for geometry optimization (hermeticity, etc.) using acts.

So the whole point of the exercise here is to verify that placing modules is feasible from python?

Overall, the findings look solid. Usage of the vector based json loading looks a bit odd, I would probably have reached for a python level loop over entries and then used the single surface converters. 

Why even load this from json at all? Any benefit over using python directly, especially since larger changes to the geometric structure (like different staggering of layers) will require structural changes to the blueprint code.

Yes—the purpose is to establish that finite sensitive modules can be placed and propagated through from Python, as groundwork for later coverage studies. JSON is not required as the design interface, and I agree that staggering and changes to layer/container structure belong in the Python construction code.

The original vector JSON load was a wheel workaround: `pyacts==47.7.0` exposes the vector/hierarchy readers but no single-surface converter binding, and directly created planes remain non-sensitive even after assigning a sensitive geometry ID. The underlying `Surface::assignIsSensitive` method was not bound.

I checked the local corrected ACTS main build. Its transform constructor is fixed, but the sensitivity setter was still missing. I added the binding and regression tests in [ACTS PR #6176](https://github.com/acts-project/acts/pull/6176). It exposes the existing C++ method and retains its guard against overriding sensitivity owned by a placement object.

The default module path in this PR now uses a Python loop over placements:
```python
surface = acts.Surface.createPlane(transform, bounds)
surface.assignIsSensitive(True)
# The Python blueprint builder assigns these surfaces to its layer nodes.
```
No module JSON is read or written on this path. JSON is an explicit compatibility/comparison control only; optional snapshots/interchange are its remaining benefit. A topology change still requires changing the Python blueprint builder.

Validation on the patched build: 32 modules; baseline and alternating-z layouts; both navigation policies; all 1,600 analytic ray comparisons and 192 propagation comparisons passed. Python and JSON IDs, navigation CSVs and propagation outputs match exactly. Four new upstream test cases fail before the patch; 20 focused tests pass afterward. After the local dependency update, the full ACTS Python Core suite also passes: **56 passed, 1 skipped**. All ACTS pre-commit hooks pass, and the original wheel controls remain reproducible.

The [response and limitations](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/docs/validation/TRK-SE03-pyacts-bindings.md), [runner](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/tools/acts_binding_probe/python_construction.py) and [retained results](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/blob/de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8/docs/validation/TRK-SE03-python-construction.json) are in commit `de395b40f4589829e6df1c5283cff56c685d77d8`. These are synthetic capability checks, not a claim of detector hermeticity or performance.

@paulgessinger - after your comment, we figured that for full flexibility - working with the`pyacts` wheel is not sufficiently flexible yet. We have established a sister repository, with a local acts installation that can be used for adding specific functionality.

The live package index and PyPI JSON report 47.7.0. The wheel supports a tested
JSON-sensitive-surface → LayerBlueprintNode → Blueprint.construct route.

seeded rays, with 45 crossings each. This completes only the binding assessment;
DES-005 TRK-SE03 and physical tracker studies remain incomplete.

Direct Transform3(translation, rotation) produced nonfinite values; pinned source
shows uninitialized storage. Angle-axis composition and JSON transforms work.
Direct geometry IDs do not make surfaces sensitive, but JSON sensitivity does.
The blueprint children getter also fails. Limitations and reproduction commands
are retained in the assessment, with public source ID SRC-PYACTS-4770-BINDINGS.
No installed wheel/upstream source was patched. No upstream message was sent.

Starting revision and branch are recorded in the paired JSON. Prior pyacts

events.text:
Used the release-pinned ACTS propagation-example sequence with the existing
module blueprint fixture, EigenStepper/Navigator and sterileLogger=False.
ROOT step writing is unavailable in this wheel, so the included OBJ step writer
provides real written positions/connectivity. No custom writer or ACTS rebuild
was required. Read-only GitHub source calls used the user's standing permission;
network failures were retried with authorized access.

The central x-y figure shows 48 negative muons from the origin in each synthetic
0/2 T field, eta=0, pT=0.1 GeV, seed42, maximum step2 mm. Barrel modules are drawn
as finite plane intersections; endcaps remain in the geometry but lie outside
the slice. Every generated track has a written path and reaches the boundary.
Independent straight/circular trajectories and finite-plane intersection sets
match all 96 propagations. There are 34/30 intersections and 2744/2959 steps.
OBJ lacks surface IDs; plotted markers are actual steps geometrically associated
with module planes, not fabricated segment intersections or simulated hits.

The writer's six-significant-digit coordinates motivate numerical tolerances
of 0.001 mm for planes/trajectories and 0.002 mm for intersection positions.
These do not set detector alignment or performance requirements. Constant field
and low momentum are visualization controls, not nODD design selections.
